bullets: Mechanisms, synthesis and the arrow language: homologous series and functional groups, electrophilic addition, SN1 and SN2 substitution, and planning a synthesis route
slides.heading: JC H2 chemistry — organic: mechanisms, synthesis and the arrow language
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we learn to read organic mechanisms as stories about electron pairs - chains and functional groups first, then addition and substitution, and finally how to chain reactions into a synthesis.

bullets: Describe homologous series and functional groups, and name the family a molecule belongs to
Explain electrophilic addition to ethene and the difference between SN1 and SN2 substitution, including their rate equations
Use curly arrows correctly and plan a short synthesis route, working backwards from the target
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap about which way a curly arrow points.

bullets: A curly arrow is drawn on almost every mechanism in this topic
Does it point toward the electrons, or away from them - and how would you know?
slides.heading: Which way does a curly arrow point?
slides.notes: Ask the class to commit to a guess before any definitions: does the arrow start at the electron-rich end or the electron-poor end? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the arrow language runs through every scene of this lesson.

bullets: Every mechanism in this lesson is explained the same way: a curly arrow tracks one pair of electrons from where the pair starts to where it ends up
Reaction type follows the electrons: pi pairs attack electrophiles in addition, lone pairs attack carbon in substitution, and synthesis chains the reactions you already know
slides.heading: One idea, eight scenes: follow the electron pairs
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: mechanisms are never memorised arrow patterns - each arrow is one electron pair moving, and the reaction type tells you where to look for it.

bullets: Methane, ethane, propane and butane form a homologous series: each member adds one CH2 group, so the whole family shares the general formula CnH2n+2
Members of a series share the same functional group and similar chemistry, with physical properties changing gradually along the chain
slides.heading: Alkanes: one CH₂ group apart
slides.notes: Follow the chain growing one CH2 group at a time and narrate the state change: same family, same general formula, one carbon longer each step. Say: the series is a family portrait, not four separate molecules to memorise.

bullets: The same three-carbon skeleton belongs to different families when a different functional group is attached: -OH makes an alcohol, -COOH makes a carboxylic acid
The functional group, not the carbon skeleton, decides the family's reactions - propan-1-ol and propanoic acid behave very differently
slides.heading: Functional groups change the family
slides.notes: Narrate the functional groups landing on the same skeleton: the carbons do not change, but the family and the chemistry do. Say: name the functional group first and you have named the reactions to expect.

bullets: Ethene's pi bond is electron-rich, so its electron pair attacks the slightly positive hydrogen of H-Br: the first curly arrow runs from the pi bond to H
The second curly arrow runs from the H-Br bond onto bromine, giving Br-, and the product is bromoethane: CH2=CH2 + HBr gives CH3CH2Br
slides.heading: Electrophilic addition to alkenes
slides.notes: Trace both curly arrows in order and name what each pair does: pi pair to hydrogen, bond pair onto bromine. Say: the arrows start where the electrons are - that sentence settles almost every arrow question in this topic.

bullets: Tertiary halogenoalkanes substitute in two steps: first the C-Br bond breaks on its own, slowly, leaving a planar carbocation and Br-
Hydroxide then attacks the carbocation fast, so the rate depends only on the halogenoalkane: rate = k[(CH3)3CBr]
slides.heading: SN1: the slow step comes first
slides.notes: Narrate the slow break first, then the fast attack. Say: the slow step is the bottleneck - hydroxide is not in it, so hydroxide cannot appear in the rate equation.

bullets: Primary halogenoalkanes substitute in one concerted step: hydroxide attacks the carbon from the back, opposite the C-Br bond, while bromide leaves
Both reactants meet in the single step, so the rate depends on both: rate = k[CH3Br][OH-]
slides.heading: SN2: one step, backside attack
slides.notes: Follow the hydroxide in from the back and the bromide out the front, all in one step through one transition state. Say: one step, two reactants, both in the rate equation - the exact opposite shape from SN1.

bullets: Real synthesis chains reactions you already know: ethene becomes bromoethane by electrophilic addition, then ethanol by nucleophilic substitution, then ethanal by partial oxidation
Retrosynthesis plans the route backwards: start from the target molecule and ask what it could be made from, one step at a time
slides.heading: One route, three steps
slides.notes: Walk the route forwards once, naming the reaction type on each arrow, then walk it backwards from ethanal. Say: every arrow in a route must be a reaction you can already explain.

bullets: The trap reading treats the curly arrow as an atom sliding along it - but atoms stay put; only electron pairs move
Read every arrow as a pair: the pair starts at a bond, a lone pair or a pi bond, and ends where the new bond forms or on the leaving atom
slides.heading: A common mistake: atoms sliding along the arrow
slides.notes: Slow down for the trap scene. Say: the bromine atom never travels along the arrow - the pair leaves the bond and ends on bromine, which is why Br- appears. Atoms stay put, pairs move.

bullets: Addition is pi electrons attacking an electrophile; substitution splits into SN1's slow carbocation step and SN2's single concerted step
Synthesis is chaining known reactions and planning backwards - and every arrow in every mechanism follows the electrons
slides.heading: Organic mechanisms in one page
slides.notes: Pull the whole lesson onto one page: addition, the two substitutions, and the route that chains them. Say: if you can say where each electron pair starts and ends, you can rebuild any mechanism in this topic.

bullets: Step 1: name each change - ethene to bromoethane adds HBr across the double bond, bromoethane to ethanol swaps Br for OH, ethanol to ethanal removes hydrogen
Step 2: match each change to a known reaction - electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution with aqueous NaOH and heat, then partial oxidation, stopping before ethanoic acid
slides.heading: Worked example: planning the ethene to ethanal route
slides.notes: Talk through the route slowly and name the reaction type on each arrow as you write it; say: work backwards from ethanal if the forwards direction stalls - the last step must be an oxidation, so the step before it must make the alcohol.

bullets: Ethene reacts with HBr. Draw the two curly arrows of the mechanism and state, for each arrow, where its electron pair starts and where it ends
Careful - a classmate says: Curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one. Explain to them where a curly arrow actually starts
slides.heading: Your turn: explain, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the pi pair first, then on the exact sentence they used to talk their classmate out of the claim: Curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one.

bullets: On your own: a tertiary halogenoalkane reacts with aqueous NaOH and the rate does not change when the NaOH concentration doubles. Name the mechanism and explain the rate evidence
Watch out for the trap one last time: Curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one. Say where the arrow in the ethene and HBr mechanism actually starts, and why
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for SN1 with the slow-step reasoning in your first answer and one clear sentence about the electron-rich pi bond in your second. Anyone repeating the claim Curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one. needs the arrow scenes again.
